summary: Project TacetField is a human-centered planning and navigation tool for crewed Mars surface missions. Mars has no GPS, maps hide steep and loose terrain, and communication lag prevents live guidance from Earth. Unlike rover planners that only measure wheel distance, Martian Map models the astronaut: it estimates oxygen use, exertion and fatigue along a route and gives Go / No-Go safety margins against life-support limits. It runs on interactive 3D terrain built from real orbital elevation data of Jezero Crater, Gale Crater and Valles Marineris, with switchable layers for optical, mineral, thermal and geologic maps. Planners can also pick a science goal, such as astrobiology or paleoclimate. A route planning tablet interface, a simulated Martian sol with shadow forecasting, and live telemetry support safer, more productive and more efficient EVAs.
details:
What it does
Martian Map is a crewed-EVA mission planner and navigator. It helps mission planners and astronauts choose where to go, judge whether a traverse is survivable, and find the most scientifically valuable targets, all on realistic 3D Martian terrain.

How it works

  1. Human-centered EVA planning. The route engine reads slope and vertical climb to estimate oxygen consumption and calorie burn. It combines slope changes, loose regolith or scree risk and the distance between rest stops into a fatigue score. It then compares the planned traverse and return against primary O₂, suit battery and scrubber limits to give a Go / No-Go margin. It also flags escarpments, steep crater walls (over 25°), boulder fields and dune drift.
  2. Science-driven targeting. The user picks a discipline and the tool highlights matching sectors and landmarks: astrobiology (lakebed clays, delta fronts, e.g. Jezero Delta Scarp and Séítah), paleoclimate (sediment layers, clays vs. sulfates), volcanic geochronology (olivine-rich units, impact melt), and hydrogeology (channels, alluvial fans, ice candidates from THEMIS night-time thermal data). Each landmark is cross-referenced with instruments such as SHERLOC, PIXL and SuperCam.
  3. Dual-mode tablet interface. Dossier mode flies the camera to a landmark to show its geology and mission history. Route mode drops waypoints, computes 3D slope-aware distances and compares multi-leg paths.
  4. 3D elevation and multispectral GIS. Terrain is generated from 16-bit orbital DEM data. Layers include HiRISE imagery, CRISM mineral spectroscopy, THEMIS thermal inertia and USGS geologic maps. Markers fade out at regional zoom levels and return as the user zooms in, and they can be hidden with one click.
  5. Martian solar simulation. A full 24-hour sol simulation shows real-time shadows, solar elevation and azimuth. This helps forecast solar-panel output, thermal drops and shadow hazards on crater walls.
  6. Telemetry and ergonomics. A cursor readout shows latitude, longitude, elevation and slope in real time. The metric scale bar updates as the camera zooms, and there is an Earth–Mars communication-latency counter and camera presets (nadir, tactical oblique, low-angle). The dark, high-contrast avionics-style UI is built for glove-friendly use.

Benefits we aim to validate.
Better astronaut safety through proactive hazard and life-support warnings, more reliable missions through clearer navigation decisions, and savings in time and oxygen through efficient routing and science targeting.

Current limitation and next steps.
The prototype uses existing orbital datasets rather than live mission-control telemetry or physical suit hardware. Next we plan to add live terrain updates, sub-meter boulder scoring, a helmet HUD and tactile glove hardware tested in simulated EVAs.

Tools we used

  • Languages: TypeScript, JavaScript (ESNext), Python 3, HTML5, CSS3, GLSL (OpenGL Shading Language)
  • 3D Graphics & GIS: Three.js (WebGL 2.0), Canvas 2D API
  • UI Framework & Styling: React 18, Tailwind CSS, PostCSS, Lucide React (tactical SVG icons)
  • Build & Development: Vite, Rollup, esbuild, Node.js, npm
  • Data Preprocessing: NumPy, Pillow (PIL) (used for processing raw NASA MOLA DEMs and raster maps)

Code was developed with assistance from Google Gemini.
